summary.title: Build Redis: Concurrent Clients [3/5]
summary.one_liner: You learn why a naive Ruby TCP server fails on repeated commands, how threads fix it, and how an IO.select-based event loop serves many clients on one thread.
takeaways: A server that stops listening to a client after one reply cannot handle a second command from that client.
Spawning a thread per client lets one server accept new clients while serving existing ones, at the cost of thread overhead.
An event loop serves many clients on one thread, but any blocking call inside it stalls every client.
IO.select can watch the server socket and client sockets together, so accept and read calls are only made when data is ready.
Replacing gets with readpartial makes the read non-blocking, though command parsing is deferred to the next article.
summary.summary: This is the third part of a series building a toy Redis clone in Ruby that answers PING. It first shows a bug where the server drops a client after one reply, then fixes it by serving each client in its own thread. The article then explains event loops with a bartender analogy, defines blocking and non-blocking calls, and introduces IO.select to watch the server and client sockets together. The final implementation uses a single-threaded select loop with readpartial, and the minitest integration tests pass against it.
